textPlacement.assessment: The revised topic row states a narrow attributed perspective on fitting, releasing, turning and two-hand movements. Its new final sentence directs attention to the movement the child repeats; it does not prescribe access to arbitrary lids or small objects. The full entry retains rings/shapes/sliding and bin-box examples, taking apart before replacing, later color/size matching, source-supported simplification of a shape sorter, nonrequired materials and explicit small-part supervision. The age context keeps distinct labels and closure variants rather than turning 18–24 into a deadline or a blanket household-closure approval. No new sensitive setup or developmental outcome claim is introduced.

The topic invitation stays within looking/listening at ordinary outdoor discoveries. The new readiness sentence now describes stopping, pointing, listening and looking with the adult, matching the invitation and the source’s interest-led noticing. The full entry preserves optional time, the child’s pace, quiet shared looking, wondering/finding out together and possibilities beyond a private garden. General indicative-age context is supported by the complete activity unit retained here. No touching/collecting recipe, water activity, weather imperative, climbing instruction or numerical readiness requirement is added.

The attributed topic row links everyday movement with current movement rather than a skill target. The revised age/readiness text follows the child’s current movements and available space. Full detail retains space-permitting indoor movement, outdoors and the source’s outdoor-space rationale for ball rolling/kicking. Longer equipment possibilities remain descriptive context with explicitly differing ages/readiness; chapter/photo/appendix bike timing is not silently merged into a progression. No apparatus construction, elevation, riding setup or adult-positioning instruction is introduced.

Both actual topic rows, in Play & discovery and A home that helps, remain a narrow unaged home-play perspective about existing favorites. The current cue concerns exploring a familiar toy, with no present-age pretend-play expectation. In the full page, the age context and first detail paragraph separately identify the creativity discussion’s around-2½-years-and-later framing. The explicit note says it is later context rather than an expectation for an 18–24-month-old. The home/school distinction, optional toy examples and small-part supervision remain visible. PDF 71’s section title and the corrected PDF 103–104 creativity reference are accurate. My two r02 findings are resolved on this exact replacement; no fantasy prohibition, psychological guarantee or detailed 3+ block activity is introduced.
